newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Fiftieth anniversary revives Wallenberg mystery.
newsitem.headline: Fiftieth anniversary revives Wallenberg mystery.

text.p: The mysterious disappearance of Swedish diplomat Raoul Wallenberg, who saved thousands of Jews during World War Two, was back in Swedish headlines on Thursday, 50 years to the day since his supposed death.
Wallenberg, who saved Jews from Nazi death camps by giving them passports or hiding them, disappeared after being arrested in January 1945 when Russian forces conquered Hungary.
Russian authorities say Wallenberg died of a heart attack in a Moscow jail on July 17, 1947, while other theories claim he was executed, died in a Soviet gulag, or is still alive, now aged 84.
"We are waiting for the truth," said Swedish newspaper Expressen.
"What happened to Raoul Wallenberg on July 17, 1947?" asked daily broadsheet Svenska Dagbladet.
Alice Breuer, 71, a Hungarian Jew, said she would have been one of the victims of the Nazi Holocaust if it had not been for Wallenberg who was posted in Budapest during the war.
As she faced a German firing squad with a group of Jews in Budapest in 1945, Wallenberg intervened, saying the group was subject to Swedish law and demanded their release.
"I would have been executed if Wallenberg had not saved us. It was a miracle. He has a place in paradise," Breuer told Expressen.
She eventually settled in Sweden on a passport issued by Wallenberg.

Investigations into Wallenberg's disappearance are still continuing, with a joint Swedish-Russian working group examining relevant documents and preparing a report for release by the end of this year.

Moscow said searches in Soviet archives since the end of the Cold War have produced nothing to contradict the official Soviet version that the Swede died of a heart attack in Moscow's Lubyanka prison.

However, Swedes have disputed the authenticity of a Soviet document which was a prison doctor's report asking for instructions from the security ministry on what to do with the body of Wallenberg. It was made public in 1957 by the Soviet Union.
"It was highly unusual for a doctor to send such a report to the security ministry," said Hans Magnusson, co-chairman of a Russian-Swedish working group on Wallenberg.
Other allegedly official documents obtained by Russian newspaper Izvestia said Wallenberg was executed on July 17, 1947 on orders from Josef Stalin.
Svenska Dagbladet said witnesses say Wallenberg was in a Soviet prison where he died in 1956.
The CIA in 1993 said Wallenberg had been working for a semi-clandestine U.S. agency which may have aroused Soviet suspicions and led to his arrest.
Surviving family members say he might still be alive.
His niece Nane Annan, wife of United Nations secretary-general Kofi Annan, said earlier this year that her family will never stop searching until they find absolute proof of his fate.
